source_text: Quod aut utrumque simul negatur, aut simul utrumque suscipitur; et cum sit in potestate utriusque reiectio, non est tamen in arbitrio alterius electio; nisi quod facilius potest illicita commixtione gravari vitio voluntatis, seminum tamen fructificatione defensa, quam fructibus eius accusatis, sexuum negotium vindicari. Non ergo fluctuatio tua, quam inter formidinem impietatemque perpeteris, novas disputandi regulas condere valebit, ut de duobus connexis unum suscipias, et quod ei adhaeret excludas. Ante leves pascentur in aethere cervi [n168] , quam post praeiudicium sumpti negetur effectio. Exercet hoc genus apostolus Paulus, cum dicit: Si mortui non resurgunt, nec Christus resurrexit. Si Christus non resurrexit, vana est fides vestra [n169] . Nunc autem Christus resurrexit; constat ergo functorum diem resurrectionem futuram. Et ut hoc ipsum breviore propter legentem inculcemus exemplo; dubitetur utrum iustum bonum sit; peto, an omne iustum, honestum esse fatearis. Quo concesso, addo aliud, utrum omne honestum, bonum quoque esse pronunties. Hoc quoque dato, te volente nolente, concludo: Si omne iustum honestum, omne honestum bonum; omne igitur iustum bonum est. Huic effecto quicumque post prima sumpta voluerit obniti, non aedificium rationis quatit, sed ipse se exponit irrisui. Ut ergo ad causam comparatio recurrat, quaeritur utrum sit in natura peccatum; petivi, concederesne nullum esse sine voluntate peccatum; assensus es, sicut tua dicta testantur. Addidi, an in parvulo putares esse voluntatem; hoc etiam denegasti. Quid sequitur tertium, si non est sine voluntate peccatum? Hoc tam certum est ut nec ab Academicis venire possit in dubium, quorum divitiae sunt nihil certum tenere. Tu ergo cum post duo prima sumpta, tertium negas, in quo est effectus duorum, non rationis fundamenta convellis, sed tuum prodis furorem.
pass_a_gloss: Which either both together is denied, or both together is taken up; and although the rejection of each is in power, nevertheless the choice of one is not in decision; except that it can more easily be weighed by a vice of will in an illicit mingling, the fruiting of seeds nevertheless having been defended, than, its fruits having been accused, the business of the sexes be claimed. Therefore your fluctuation, which you suffer between fear and impiety, will not be able to found new rules of disputing, so that of two connected things you take up one and exclude what clings to it. Sooner will light stags feed in the ether, than after the prior judgment of things taken up the effect is denied. The apostle Paul exercises this kind, when he says: If the dead do not rise, neither did Christ rise. If Christ did not rise, your faith is vain. But now Christ has risen; it stands therefore that a resurrection of those who have died will be future. And that we may impress this itself by a shorter example for the reader; let it be doubted whether the just is good; I ask whether you confess that every just thing is honorable. Which having been granted, I add another, whether you pronounce that every honorable thing is also good. This also having been given, you willing or unwilling, I conclude: If every just thing is honorable, every honorable thing good; every just thing therefore is good. Whoever after the first things taken up shall have wanted to resist this effect does not shake the building of reason, but exposes himself to mockery. Therefore that the comparison may run back to the cause, it is asked whether there is sin in nature; I asked whether you would grant that there is no sin without will; you assented, as your sayings testify. I added, whether you thought there is will in a little one; this also you denied. What third follows, if there is not sin without will? This is so certain that it cannot even come into doubt from the Academics, whose riches are to hold nothing certain. You therefore when after the two first things taken up you deny the third, in which is the effect of the two, do not tear the foundations of reason, but you betray your fury.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS parvulus; Blaise infants as Julian's test case
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Either both are denied together or both are accepted together. Although one can reject both, one cannot choose only one. It is, however, easier for an unlawful union to be burdened with the fault of will while the fruitfulness of its seeds remains defended, than for the sexual act to be vindicated while its fruits are accused. Your wavering between fear and impiety will therefore not establish new rules of argument, allowing you to accept one of two connected things and exclude what belongs to it. “Light-footed deer will graze in the sky” (Virgil, Eclogues 1.59) before a conclusion can be denied after its premise has settled the matter.

The apostle Paul uses this form of argument when he says, “If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. If Christ has not risen, your faith is empty” (1 Corinthians 15:16–17). But now Christ has risen; therefore it is certain that a day of resurrection awaits the dead (compare 1 Corinthians 15:20–23). To press this same point upon the reader with a shorter example: suppose there is doubt whether what is just is good. I ask whether you acknowledge that everything just is honorable. Once that is granted, I add another question: do you also pronounce everything honorable good? Once that too is granted, whether you like it or not, I conclude: if everything just is honorable, and everything honorable is good, then everything just is good. Anyone who tries to resist this conclusion after accepting the first premises does not shake reason’s structure but exposes himself to ridicule.

To bring the comparison back to the case: the question is whether sin exists in nature. I asked whether you would concede that no sin exists without will. You agreed, as your own words testify. I added whether you thought an infant possessed will. You denied this too. What follows as the third point, if sin does not exist without will? This is so certain that it cannot be doubted even by the Academics, whose wealth consists in holding nothing certain. So when you deny the third point after the first two premises, although it contains their conclusion, you do not overturn the foundations of reason: you reveal your frenzy.

choices.why: Julian defends marital union (commixtio) as God's work, not the devil's property.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
